core.text: Three common verbs make **the future of the irregular verbs (ero = I will be, potero = I will be able, ibo = I will go)** their own way. *Sum* uses a special stem *er-* with the ordinary endings: *erō, eris, erit, erimus, eritis, erunt*. *Possum* is just *pot-* + that: *poterō, poteris, poterit*. *Eō* keeps its stem *ī-* and takes the -b- future: *ībō, ībis, ībit, ībimus, ībitis, ībunt*. Latin name: *futūrum verbōrum anomalōrum*.
The future in English is *will* + verb: *I will be, I will be able, I will go*.
erō / poterō like the present endings of sum on er-; ībō like laudābō. Volō, nōlō, mālō and ferō are regular third-conjugation futures: volet, nōlet, mālet, feret.

invented.la: Crās Rōmam ībimus et amīcōs vidēbimus.
invented.en: Tomorrow we will go to Rome and see our friends.

core.text: *erit* (will be) looks like the ending of **the future perfect (the 'will have done' tense)**: *laudāverit* (will have praised). If *er-* stands alone it is the future of *sum*; if it is glued to a perfect stem (*laudāv-erit*) it is the future perfect.

more.text: From the learner's notes (week 20): compounds of *sum* follow it (*aderō* I will be present, *aberit* he will be away), and compounds of *eō* follow *eō* (*redībit* he will return, *exībit* he will go out).
Watch the two imperfects that rhyme with these futures: *eram* (I was) versus *erō* (I will be); *ībam* (I was going) versus *ībō*. The vowel after the stem decides.
